title: Obligation, permission and advice
tagline: Rules you can't break, rules you don't need to follow, and advice that's just strongly worded.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations
Reading & Use of English Part 1 — multiple-choice cloze
Speaking Part 3 — discussing rules and recommendations
why: Spanish speakers often confuse mustn't with don't have to — one forbids, the other simply says something isn't necessary — and that single mix-up can flip the meaning of a whole sentence. B2 First tests this contrast directly, along with the past forms (had to, should have) that students often forget exist.

rows.label: Meaning
cells: it is forbidden — a rule against it
it isn't necessary — but you can if you want

rows.label: Where the rule comes from
cells: no external rule, so it's optional

rows.label: Example
cells: You mustn't use your phone in the exam.
You don't have to bring a calculator, there's one for you.

head: Form
Meaning
Example
rows: must / have to
obligation now (must = the speaker's own rule; have to = an external rule)
I must remember to charge my phone. / We have to wear a uniform.
mustn't
prohibition — it's forbidden
You mustn't run near the pool.
needn't / don't have to
no obligation — it's optional
You needn't bring lunch, it's provided.
should / ought to
advice or a recommendation
You should ask Miss Vega for an extension.
had better
strong advice, often with a warning of consequences
You'd better hurry or you'll miss the bus.
be allowed to / be permitted to
permission, in any tense
Are we allowed to use dictionaries in the test?
had to / didn't have to (past)
past obligation / past lack of obligation
We had to queue for an hour. We didn't have to pay.
should have / shouldn't have + participle
criticism or regret about the past
You shouldn't have left it until the last minute.

use.point: Present obligation: must vs have to

examples.text: I must remember to email Miss Vega before Friday.
Students have to wear the school jumper in winter.
examples.note: an external rule, not the speaker's opinion

examples.text: You have to show your ID card to enter the library.
You mustn't use a phone during the listening exam.
You don't have to bring your own racket — the club has spares.
We needn't hurry; the gates don't open until six.
examples.note: no obligation, said at the moment

examples.text: You should ask for help instead of guessing every answer.
Nadia ought to practise her presentation one more time.
You'd better finish that essay tonight — the deadline is tomorrow.

use.point: Looking back: past obligation, permission and regret

examples.text: We had to rewrite the whole report after the printer failed.
Sofia didn't have to pay for the trip — she won a scholarship.
Liam should have checked the timetable before leaving home.

watch_out.wrong: You mustn't bring a laptop if you don't want to — it's your choice.
watch_out.right: You don't have to bring a laptop if you don't want to.
watch_out.why: Mustn't forbids something; use don't have to when there's simply no obligation.

watch_out.wrong: Yesterday, we must hand in the forms before lunch.
watch_out.right: Yesterday, we had to hand in the forms before lunch.
watch_out.why: Must has no past form — use had to for a past obligation.

watch_out.wrong: You should to ask the teacher first.
watch_out.why: Should, like other modals, is followed by the bare infinitive, never to.

watch_out.wrong: I shouldn't have go to bed so late.
watch_out.right: I shouldn't have gone to bed so late.
watch_out.why: Should have takes a past participle, not the base form.
Be allowed to needs to before the infinitive — unlike modal verbs.

watch_out.wrong: You had better to call your mum now.
watch_out.right: You'd better call your mum now.
watch_out.why: Had better is followed directly by the bare infinitive, with no to.

dialogue.title: Rules for the science trip
dialogue.context: Miss Vega is going over the rules for the trip to the coast with Sofia, Liam and Nadia before they set off.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Right, before we go — everyone must wear a life jacket near the water. No exceptions.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Even for just looking at the tide pools? We don't have to go far in.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: It doesn't matter — you mustn't go near the rocks without one.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Understood. Do we have to bring our own snorkels, or does the centre provide them?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: You needn't bring anything — it's all included. But you should bring sun cream.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: I should have packed mine already, actually — I keep forgetting.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: You'd better do it tonight, then. Also, phones aren't allowed during the boat trip.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Seriously? Last year we didn't have to hand ours in.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: The rules changed after someone dropped one overboard. You mustn't risk it this time.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Fair enough. We should get moving — the bus leaves in ten minutes.

items.sentence: You ___ shout in the library — other people are studying.
items.why: a prohibition, not simply optional → mustn't

items.sentence: We ___ bring our own tents — the school provides them.
items.why: no obligation, it's optional → don't have to

items.sentence: Liam ___ finish his project by Friday, or he'll lose marks.
items.why: a firm outside requirement → have to

items.sentence: You look exhausted — you ___ go to bed earlier tonight.
items.why: strong advice with a consequence → had better

items.sentence: Yesterday, we ___ wait an hour because the bus was delayed.
items.why: past obligation → had to (must has no past form)

items.sentence: Sofia ___ the results earlier — she was so anxious all weekend.
items.why: criticism or regret about a past action → should have + participle

items.sentence: ___ we use calculators in this part of the exam?
items.why: asking about permission → be allowed to

items.sentence: You ___ worry about the interview — you're completely prepared.

practice.instructions: Complete each sentence with the correct modal form.

items.sentence: Passengers ___ (must/not) leave luggage unattended at any time.
You ___ (not/have to) pay for the museum tour — it's free for students.
We ___ (have to) show our passports twice at the airport last week.
Mateo ___ (should) practise his lines more before the play.
I think Nadia ___ (should/apologise) to her sister yesterday, but she didn't.
You ___ (had better) call the coach before he leaves without you.
___ (be/allowed to) students bring snacks into the exam hall?

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first. Use the word given. Do not change it. Use between two and five words.

items.first: It is forbidden to take photographs inside the museum.
It isn't necessary for you to bring a packed lunch.
It would be a good idea for Liam to apologise to the coach.
It was necessary for us to queue for over an hour.
It was a mistake for Sofia not to save her work before the crash.
Are students permitted to leave the classroom during the exam?

summary: Must / have to: obligation now — must for the speaker's own decision, have to for an outside rule.
Mustn't forbids; don't have to / needn't just means it isn't necessary — the two are opposites, not synonyms.
Should / ought to / had better: advice, from mild to strong, with had better warning of a consequence.
In the past, must becomes had to, and should have / shouldn't have + participle expresses regret or criticism.
Be allowed to needs to before the infinitive; true modals (must, should, had better) never do.
